---
title: "Soil chemistry and retention exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Exchange amount

A 0.100 kg soil has CEC 20.0 cmolc/kg. If all sites were occupied by Mg²⁺, how many moles of Mg would occupy them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Convert cmol of charge to mol of charge, then divide by two.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Total charge = 20.0 × 0.01 × 0.100 = **0.0200 mol charge**. Mg²⁺ amount = **0.0100 mol**. This is an idealised capacity state, not an aqueous concentration.
:::

## 2. Base saturation

A soil has CEC 12.0 cmolc/kg and base-cation occupation 9.00 cmolc/kg. Calculate base saturation. Does the result specify soil-water pH?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Divide occupied base charge by total exchange charge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Base saturation = **75.0%**. It does not uniquely set pH; mineralogy, exchange selectivity, solution composition, other acid–base reactions, and the measurement method matter.
:::

## 3. A carbonate inventory

A soil contains 0.0100 mol accessible CaCO₃. For a specified complete neutralisation endpoint, take CaCO₃ + 2 H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂* + H₂O. How much acid can this inventory consume?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use the two-equivalent coefficient for the stated endpoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The stoichiometric inventory is **0.0200 mol H⁺ equivalents**. Real protection also depends on dissolution rate, accessibility, gas exchange, and the actual final state.
:::

## 4. Compare two soils

Two soils have equal pH but one is rich in organic matter and exchange-active clay while the other is coarse quartz sand. What would you measure before predicting their responses to an acid input?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Measure inventories and pathways, not only pH.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Compare CEC under stated conditions, base saturation, carbonate and weatherable minerals, organic matter, water flow, and aluminium/iron chemistry. Equal pH is not evidence of equal buffering or solute retention.
:::

## Explore: same pH, different reserves {#explore}

Predict which soil is first to release aluminium when both receive
5.0 cmol~c~/kg of acid: Soil A (sandy podzol) or Soil B (clay loam), both at
pH about 5. Then change one inventory at a time.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="soilbuffer" role="group" aria-label="Soil acid-neutralising reserves: carbonate, exchangeable base cations and aluminium">
<p>Reference case: Soil B (CEC 20.0, base cations 14.2 cmolc/kg, base saturation 71 %) after 5.0 cmolc/kg of acid keeps 9.2 cmolc/kg of base cations (46 %). Soil A (CEC 3.0, base cations 1.7 cmolc/kg) runs out after 1.7 cmolc/kg, so the remaining 3.3 cmolc/kg is buffered by aluminium.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/soilbuffer.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Soil B**, then **Soil A**. For each, how much acid can be
neutralised before aluminium takes over? Check the base saturation after
5.0 cmol~c~/kg of acid by hand.

**E2.** Choose **Exercise 2** and confirm your base saturation. Then raise CEC
while keeping the base cations fixed. Which changes: base saturation, the
reserve, or both?

**E3.** Choose **Soil A, limed**. How many cmol~c~/kg does 2.0 cmol/kg of CaCO₃
add, and why is it twice the number of moles? Which reserve is used first in
this model?

### Model conditions and hand check

The two soils are the constructed Soil A and Soil B from the lecture. Acid is
counted in cmol~c~/kg and consumed in a fixed order: accessible CaCO₃ first
(2 equivalents per mole, CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + CO₂\* + H₂O), then exchangeable
base cations (one equivalent of bases leaves per equivalent of acid), and then
aluminium. CEC is held constant; the sites given up by base cations are taken by
Al³⁺ and H⁺. Slow weathering, uptake by plants, rates, flow paths and pH are not
modelled. For Soil B after 5.0 cmol~c~/kg: 14.2 − 5.0 = **9.2 cmol~c~/kg** of
base cations remain, and base saturation falls from 14.2/20.0 = 71 % to
9.2/20.0 = **46 %**. If those 5.0 cmol~c~/kg left as Ca²⁺, that is
**2.5 cmol Ca/kg**. Soil A has only 1.7 cmol~c~/kg, so **3.3 cmol~c~/kg** of
the same acid is buffered by aluminium.
